doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
title: Never a sideman again: owning his music and the Warner advance
summary: Once he began recording as a leader he never recorded for anyone else, published his own music, and says he got a $30,000 advance from Warner Brothers through George Avakian.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Okay, so we’ll back into the timeline. We’re in the ‘60s. You’ve now formed Wide World of Music.
Yeah.

Now since the early ‘50s you’ve been a bandleader and you probably just cherry picked the assignments that you would serve as a sideman. So Lena when she went to Europe you took that one, but at this point is it pretty much in your mind that you’re a leader, that’s your identity?

Well I’ll tell you something man, when I did my first record, my trio record, when I started recording for myself, I never recorded for anybody else ever. Haven’t been a sideman, ever. Everything I’ve done, it’s been me.

You know, I was hip to that period, you know. Everybody that wanted me to record with them, you know, which before then I recorded with anybody, you know, but once I started for myself, that was it man.
Why?
Well several reasons. Number one, I wanted to play my music. Number two, I owned my music. I publish my own music. Does that tell you why?
Complete control.
Complete control. So that’s why.
And you were lucky enough or fortunate enough -­
Fortunate enough.
To team up with record companies that allowed you to continue.
To do that.
They understood your vision, they supported you.
Right. Well I sold records.

You made them money. MR.HAMILTON: I made them money. I made them money, you know. You know, you talk about, Miles getting a lot of money from Columbia, man, when I went with Warner Brothers, George Avakian, right, I got a $30,000 advance you know.
You’re talking about what year, the late ‘50s?
Yeah.
Dang, so you beat out Miles and he got chump change coming -­
But anyway, you know, they got it back.
Oh, yes. What was it like working with George Avakian, because he’s still around?

George is still around, yeah. George is cool man. We’re still good friends. We’re still good friends. We talk every once in a while. Every once in a while he’ll call me or I’ll call him. We’ve been cool, you dig?

That’s good. I mean, yeah, the last time I talked to George he talked a lot about, you know, his relationship with Miles, you know, and why he did certain things and wouldn’t do certain things with Miles.
